### Problem: Wiggle Sort II {#sec-part-p4-a}

::: {.p-statement}
An array `nums` of $n$ integers ($1 \le n \le 5 \cdot 10^4$, $0 \le \text{nums}[i] \le 5000$). Reorder it in place so that

$$\text{nums}[0] < \text{nums}[1] > \text{nums}[2] < \text{nums}[3] > \cdots$$

that is, every odd index is strictly larger than both of its neighbours. The input is guaranteed to have an answer. Follow-up: $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra memory.

Source: [LC 324 · Wiggle Sort II](https://leetcode.com/problems/wiggle-sort-ii/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}

Example: `[1,5,1,1,6,4]` → `[1,6,1,5,1,4]`; `[1,3,2,2,3,1]` → `[2,3,1,3,1,2]`. Other valid answers are accepted.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Deal the larger half of the values into the odd slots (the peaks) and the smaller half into the even slots (the valleys). Every comparison then holds with $\ge$; it can only fail by equality, when copies of the middle value land next to each other. Dealing both halves in decreasing order pushes those copies to opposite ends of the array, and then they can meet only if the middle value occurs so often that no answer exists. A median, a three-way partition read through the index map $t \mapsto (1+2t) \bmod (n \mid 1)$, gives the same arrangement in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra memory.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Try every arrangement.** Enumerate the distinct permutations and return the first strict wiggle. $O(n! \cdot n)$: only an oracle for $n \le 8$.
2. **Sort, then deal reversed halves.** Sort; let $h = \lceil n/2 \rceil$. Write the small half `s[:h]` in *decreasing* order into slots $0, 2, 4, \ldots$ and the large half `s[h:]` in decreasing order into slots $1, 3, 5, \ldots$. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ extra for the sorted copy.
3. **Median + virtual-index three-way partition.** Find the median value $m$ with quickselect (@sec-salgo-a4-select). Then run the three-way partition with order `[> m | == m | < m]`, but on the *virtual* array whose slot $t$ is the real cell $(1 + 2t) \bmod (n \mid 1)$. Virtual slots $0, 1, \ldots$ are the real cells $1, 3, 5, \ldots$ and then $0, 2, 4, \ldots$, so the partition fills the peaks with the large values first and the valleys with the small values last. $O(n)$ expected time, $O(1)$ extra.

**Why forms 2 and 3 work (one lemma).** Let $L = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ be the number of odd slots. Both forms put a sequence $U$ into the odd slots and a sequence $D$ into the even slots, left to right, with $\min U \ge \max D$. Every neighbour pair is one odd and one even slot, so every comparison holds with $\ge$, and it is strict unless both cells hold the same value $v = \min U = \max D$. In both forms the copies of $v$ in $U$ come *last* (they are the smallest of $U$) and the copies in $D$ come *first*. If $a$ copies sit in the last $a$ odd slots, the leftmost is cell $2(L-a)+1$; if $b$ copies sit in the first $b$ even slots, the rightmost is cell $2(b-1)$. They touch only if $2(L-a)+1 \le 2(b-1)+1$, that is $a + b \ge L + 1$: the value $v$ occurs at least $\lfloor n/2\rfloor + 1$ times.

No such value can sit in both halves when an answer exists. Equal values are never adjacent in a strict wiggle, so a value occurs at most $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ times. For even $n$ that is $L$, a contradiction. For odd $n$ a value with $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ copies must fill *every* even slot, so it is smaller than everything else: it is the minimum, all its copies are in $D$, and none is in $U$. $\blacksquare$

For form 3 also check the sizes: with $m$ the lower median `sorted(nums)[(n-1)//2]`, at most $L$ values are $> m$ and at most $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ are $< m$, so the "greater" block fits in the peaks and the "less" block in the valleys.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Try every arrangement

::: {.form-next}
The definition as code: walk the distinct permutations in order and return the first strict wiggle, or `None`. Exponential, so it is the oracle for tiny inputs, and it is also how we learn which small inputs have no answer at all.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
from itertools import permutations


def is_wiggle(a):
    return all((a[i] < a[i + 1]) if i % 2 == 0 else (a[i] > a[i + 1]) for i in range(len(a) - 1))


def wiggle_brute(nums):
    for p in sorted(set(permutations(nums))):
        if is_wiggle(p):
            return list(p)
    return None


assert wiggle_brute([1, 5, 1, 1, 6, 4]) == [1, 4, 1, 5, 1, 6]   # first in lexicographic order
assert wiggle_brute([2, 2, 2, 1]) is None                       # three 2s cannot be kept apart
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
bool isWiggle(const vector<int>& a) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i + 1 < a.size(); ++i)
        if (i % 2 == 0 ? !(a[i] < a[i + 1]) : !(a[i] > a[i + 1])) return false;
    return true;
}
bool wiggleBrute(vector<int>& a) {            // a becomes the first wiggle, if any
    sort(a.begin(), a.end());
    do { if (isWiggle(a)) return true; } while (next_permutation(a.begin(), a.end()));
    return false;
}
```
:::

#### Sort, then deal reversed halves

::: {.form-next}
Sort, split at $h = \lceil n/2 \rceil$, and deal each half into its slots in *decreasing* order. The direction matters. Dealing in increasing order also gives a $\ge$ wiggle, but it puts the small half's copies of the middle value at its right end and the large half's copies at its left end, side by side in the middle of the array: on $[1, 2, 2, 3]$ it produces $[1, 2, 2, 3]$, and the two $2$s touch.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("wiggle", "dupfail")
    assert str(final) == "[1, 2, 2, 3]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

Reversing both halves sends the copies to opposite ends, which is the lemma's shape: on $[1, 2, 2, 3]$ it gives $[2, 3, 1, 2]$, and on the second sample:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("wiggle", "sortrev")
    assert str(final) == "[2, 3, 1, 3, 1, 2]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-0324-sortrev
def wiggle_sorted(nums):
    s = sorted(nums)
    h = (len(s) + 1) // 2
    nums[0::2] = s[:h][::-1]          # valleys: small half, largest first
    nums[1::2] = s[h:][::-1]          # peaks:   large half, largest first
    return nums


def wiggle_front(nums):               # the increasing deal, for contrast
    s = sorted(nums)
    h = (len(s) + 1) // 2
    nums[0::2], nums[1::2] = s[:h], s[h:]
    return nums


assert wiggle_front([1, 2, 2, 3]) == [1, 2, 2, 3] and not is_wiggle([1, 2, 2, 3])
assert wiggle_sorted([1, 2, 2, 3]) == [2, 3, 1, 2]
for _ in range(1500):
    nums = [random.randint(0, 3) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 8))]
    if wiggle_brute(nums) is None:
        continue                      # the statement guarantees an answer
    out = wiggle_sorted(list(nums))
    assert is_wiggle(out) and sorted(out) == sorted(nums), nums
assert wiggle_sorted([1, 3, 2, 2, 3, 1]) == [2, 3, 1, 3, 1, 2]   # the board sample
assert wiggle_sorted([1, 5, 1, 1, 6, 4]) == [1, 6, 1, 5, 1, 4]   # official sample 1
print("wiggle_sorted OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
void wiggleSorted(vector<int>& nums) {
    vector<int> s(nums);
    sort(s.begin(), s.end());
    int n = (int)s.size(), h = (n + 1) / 2;
    for (int i = 0; i < h; ++i) nums[2 * i] = s[h - 1 - i];          // small half, decreasing
    for (int i = 0; i < n - h; ++i) nums[2 * i + 1] = s[n - 1 - i];  // large half, decreasing
}

int main() {
    vector<int> v{1, 5, 1, 1, 6, 4};
    wiggleSorted(v);                                                  // {1, 6, 1, 5, 1, 4}
    return (v[1] == 6 && v[5] == 4) ? 0 : 1;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `nums[0::2] = s[:h][::-1]` is the whole trick: slot $2i$ receives `s[h-1-i]` and slot $2i+1$ receives `s[n-1-i]`. The random test filters out inputs without an answer using the oracle, exactly the promise the statement makes; on every remaining input the deal is a strict wiggle, as the lemma says.

#### Median + virtual-index partition

::: {.form-next}
Two changes remove the sort and the copy. First, a strict wiggle only needs to know, for each value, whether it is above, at or below the median $m$, and quickselect finds $m$ in expected $O(n)$ time. Second, instead of partitioning into a separate array and then dealing, run the three-way partition directly through the index map $A(t) = (1 + 2t) \bmod (n \mid 1)$: virtual slot $t$ is the real cell $A(t)$. The partition puts `> m` first, then `== m`, then `< m`, in virtual order, which is peaks first and valleys last. One pass, $O(1)$ extra.

Why $n \mid 1$ (that is, $n$ if $n$ is odd and $n + 1$ if it is even): the modulus must be odd for $t \mapsto 1 + 2t$ to hit every cell exactly once (@sec-part-virtual). On the sample, $n = 6$ and the modulus is $7$: virtual slots $0..5$ are real cells $1, 3, 5, 0, 2, 4$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("wiggle", "virtual")
    assert str(final) == "[2, 3, 1, 3, 1, 2]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-0324-virtual
def quickselect(a, k):
    """Value of rank k (0-based) in a; rearranges a in place. Expected O(n)."""
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while True:
        p = a[random.randint(lo, hi)]
        lt, i, gt = lo, lo, hi                   # three-way partition of a[lo..hi] around p
        while i <= gt:
            if a[i] < p:
                a[lt], a[i] = a[i], a[lt]
                lt += 1
                i += 1
            elif a[i] > p:
                a[i], a[gt] = a[gt], a[i]
                gt -= 1
            else:
                i += 1
        if k < lt:
            hi = lt - 1
        elif k > gt:
            lo = gt + 1
        else:
            return p


def virtual_partition(nums, m):
    """Three-way partition [> m | == m | < m] over virtual slots t -> (1 + 2t) % (n | 1)."""
    n = len(nums)
    w = n | 1

    def A(t):
        return (1 + 2 * t) % w

    i, j, k = 0, 0, n - 1
    while j <= k:
        if nums[A(j)] > m:
            nums[A(i)], nums[A(j)] = nums[A(j)], nums[A(i)]
            i += 1
            j += 1
        elif nums[A(j)] < m:
            nums[A(j)], nums[A(k)] = nums[A(k)], nums[A(j)]
            k -= 1
        else:
            j += 1
    return nums


def wiggle_sort(nums):
    m = quickselect(nums, (len(nums) - 1) // 2)
    return virtual_partition(nums, m)


for _ in range(1500):
    nums = [random.randint(0, 3) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 8))]
    if wiggle_brute(nums) is None:
        continue
    out = wiggle_sort(list(nums))
    assert is_wiggle(out) and sorted(out) == sorted(nums), nums
for _ in range(300):                             # larger n: agrees with form 2 on solvability
    nums = [random.randint(0, 12) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 60))]
    assert is_wiggle(wiggle_sort(list(nums))) == is_wiggle(wiggle_sorted(list(nums)))
assert virtual_partition([1, 3, 2, 2, 3, 1], 2) == [2, 3, 1, 3, 1, 2]   # the board sample
assert is_wiggle(wiggle_sort([1, 5, 1, 1, 6, 4]))
print("wiggle_sort OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
void wiggleSort(vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = (int)nums.size(), w = n | 1;
    nth_element(nums.begin(), nums.begin() + (n - 1) / 2, nums.end());
    int m = nums[(n - 1) / 2];
    auto A = [w](int t) { return (1 + 2 * t) % w; };
    int i = 0, j = 0, k = n - 1;
    while (j <= k) {
        if (nums[A(j)] > m)      swap(nums[A(i++)], nums[A(j++)]);
        else if (nums[A(j)] < m) swap(nums[A(j)], nums[A(k--)]);
        else                     ++j;
    }
}

int main() {
    vector<int> v{1, 3, 2, 2, 3, 1};
    wiggleSort(v);
    for (int i = 0; i + 1 < (int)v.size(); ++i)
        if (i % 2 == 0 ? !(v[i] < v[i + 1]) : !(v[i] > v[i + 1])) return 1;
    return 0;
}
```
:::
:::

**Reading it line by line.** Three things carry the proof.

1. **The median.** Quickselect returns the lower median; any value with at most $L$ elements above it and at most $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ below it would do. The statement's follow-up asks for $O(n)$ time: quickselect gives that on average, and the median-of-medians pivot rule makes it worst-case linear at a larger constant (@sec-salgo-a4-select).
2. **The reversed order.** The partition puts the *greater* values first because virtual slots start with the peaks.
3. **The map.** For $n = 5$ the modulus is $5$ and the cells are $1, 3, 0, 2, 4$; for $n = 6$ it is $7$ and the cells are $1, 3, 5, 0, 2, 4$. In both cases the first $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ virtual slots are the odd cells, so the result has exactly the lemma's shape.

::: {.p-complexity}
**Try every arrangement**: $O(n! \cdot n)$ time. **Sort, then deal reversed halves**: $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ extra for the sorted copy. **Median + virtual-index partition**: $O(n)$ expected time (quickselect plus one partition pass), $O(1)$ extra; worst-case $O(n)$ with a median-of-medians pivot.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- **$n = 1$**: nothing to compare; every form leaves the array alone.
- **$n = 2$**: the answer is (smaller, larger); in form 3 the median is the smaller value, which goes to virtual slot $1$, real cell $0$.
- **Many copies of the median**: $[1, 2, 2, 2]$ has no answer (three $2$s in four cells must touch), so the statement never gives it, and the lemma shows that this is the only way the deal can fail. With one copy fewer it works: $[1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3]$ becomes $[2, 3, 1, 2, 1, 2]$.
- **Odd $n$ with the minimum $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ times**, e.g. $[1, 1, 1, 2, 3]$: valid answer $[1, 3, 1, 2, 1]$; the minimum fills every valley.
- **Increasing deal on even $n$**: fails on $[1, 2, 2, 3]$; it happens to be correct for every odd $n$, which is why a test with only odd lengths would not catch it.
:::
